note: Cases written before the skill. Each failure_mode is what actually happened on the CMAS build without these checks.

evals.prompt: We're starting a new web app for our department next week. Here's the proposal PDF and a first Prisma schema. What should we check before we start coding?
evals.context: Schema models several institutions (Institution, Membership) while the proposal says the system serves one faculty. Grading formula is described in words only.
evals.expected: Runs the before-design checklist: compares every schema boundary against the written objective and flags the multi-tenant tables as unrequested scope; asks for the calculation rule to be signed off with a worked example and a hand-computed sheet; asks for a baseline measurement of the current manual process. Reports blocking items first.
evals.failure_mode: Multi-institution schema was found only after design work had started; a whole inserted task cost about one sprint and every document had to be revised. Two readings of 'weight' differed by 20 points and blocked the calculation tests.

evals.prompt: Every page in our app takes 2-6 seconds to load. Backend is Fastify + Prisma on Supabase. Make it faster.
evals.context: Database in a distant region, transaction pooler on port 6543 with pgbouncer=true, read-only queries wrapped in prisma.$transaction([...]), one dashboard request per student.
evals.expected: Measures before changing anything (a no-DB health endpoint vs DB endpoints, query log, per-query round-trip time). Identifies round trips, not payload size, as the cost. Checks region, pooler mode, batched read transactions, N+1 per-row requests, and localhost IPv6 fallback on Windows. Proposes fixes in order of measured effect and re-measures after each.
evals.failure_mode: Without measuring, the first guess was 'the query is heavy'. The real causes were 250 ms per round trip to Tokyo, 4 round trips per query through the transaction pooler, sequential reads inside $transaction, and 40 requests for a 40-student class.

evals.prompt: Our CI has been green for weeks and we're about to merge to main. Anything we should double check?
evals.context: CI has actually been failing at npm ci because .nvmrc pins Node 20 and a dependency needs Node 22+. main has no branch protection. Coverage threshold is configured but CI runs test, not test:coverage.
evals.expected: Does not trust 'green' without looking at the latest run of each required job. Checks runtime version parity across .nvmrc, engines, CI and Dockerfiles; whether CI is a required check; whether each gate can be shown to fail (break it on a throwaway branch). Flags the unenforced coverage threshold.
evals.failure_mode: CI failed silently for three weeks; no lint, test or build result in that window was real. PRs with red CI could still be merged.

evals.prompt: Can you write up what went wrong on this project and what we learned? It's for our final report.
evals.context: A repository with about 100 commits, progress reports in docs/, and several past agent sessions.
evals.expected: Uses the retrospective method: reads git history oldest-first including commit bodies, reads progress/decision docs, searches past sessions; separates problem / cause / fix / lesson; labels what was read in full versus inferred from snippets; writes the result to a lessons file rather than only to chat; names what was not covered.
evals.failure_mode: A summary built from commit titles alone misses the causes (many commits titled 'Refactor code structure for improved readability'), and claims read as verified when they were inferred.

evals.prompt: Fix the typo in the README heading.
evals.expected: Skill does not trigger, or if consulted, states that no checklist applies and makes the edit.
evals.failure_mode: Over-applying a checklist to a one-line change is ceremony.
